chapter.title: Inspecting the work: the 3 checks before you trust a build

cards.body:
It's the end of the day and the builder says the kitchen is done. **You don't sign off from the doorway.** You walk in, turn on every tap, open every cupboard, ask what got done today, and pin a note to the wall for tomorrow's crew: *no more surprises with the plumbing.*

Three checks, every time, before you trust the work.
cards.simpler: It's the end of the day. The builder says the kitchen is finished. **You don't sign off from the doorway.** You walk in. You turn on every tap and open every cupboard. You ask what got done today. Then you pin a note to the wall for tomorrow's crew: no more surprises with the plumbing. Do these three checks every time, before you trust the work.

cards.prompt: Claude says: *Done! The 'Clear all' button now empties your shopping list.* What's your first move?

options.text: Say thanks and ask for the next feature.
Open the app and click 'Clear all' yourself, like a user would.
Ask Claude to read its own code again and double-check.

whyNot.a: That's taking the builder's word for the walkthrough: you haven't seen the tap run yet.
whyNot.c: That's asking the builder to inspect the builder. Your own click takes 5 seconds and catches more.

cards.reteach: Claude saying *done* means it believes the code is right. It has not clicked the button. You are the only one in the room who can act like a real user, so that comes first.

cards.title: Check 1 and 2: click it, then ask for the list
cards.body:
**Test as a user first.** Open the app in your browser and do the thing you asked for, start to finish. Not the code, the app. If a button was added, click it. If a form was added, fill it in with something silly and submit it.

Then ask the builder for the day's report: *List every file you changed and what you changed in each, in plain words.* Claude will give you a short list.

Read it looking for one thing: a file you didn't expect. That surprise is where the hidden damage usually lives.
cards.simpler: **Try the app yourself first.** Open it in your browser and do the whole thing you asked for. The app, not the code. If a button was added, click it. If a form was added, type something silly into it and send it. Then ask Claude for a plain list of every file it changed and what changed in each. Read that list for one thing: a file you didn't expect. That surprise is where hidden damage hides.

cards.title: The 3-file surprise
cards.body:
You ask Claude to add a 'Clear all' button to a shopping-list app. Claude says done. You click it: the list empties. Good.

Then you ask for the change list. Claude names 3 files: the page, the styling, and the file that saves the list between visits. You never mentioned saving. One question, *why that third file?*, and Claude admits it rewrote the save function 'while it was in there'. Items now vanish on refresh. **Caught in 40 seconds**, before you'd moved on and forgotten.
cards.simpler: You ask Claude to add a 'Clear all' button to a shopping-list app. Claude says done. You click it. The list empties. Then you ask what files changed. Claude names three: the page, the styling, and the file that saves your list between visits. You never mentioned saving. You ask why that third file. Claude admits it also rewrote the save code. Now items vanish when you refresh. **Caught in 40 seconds**, before you moved on and forgot.

cards.prompt: You asked for a dark-mode toggle. Claude's change list shows 4 files. One is the file that handles sign-in, which you never mentioned. What do you do?

options.text: Nothing. The toggle works, so the build is fine.
Ask: *Why did you change the sign-in file, and what exactly did you change?*
Ask Claude to delete the sign-in file so nothing's hidden in it.

whyNot.a: That's check 1 only. The toggle working says nothing about what happened to sign-in.
whyNot.c: That's panic, not inspection. Ask first; the change may be harmless, or easy to undo.

cards.reteach: The change list is a map of where the builder went. A room you didn't send it into is the first room you look in. Ask why, then test that room too.

cards.title: Check 3: the note pinned to the wall
cards.body:
Every new Claude Code session starts with a blank memory. Yesterday's 'please don't touch the save file' is gone. The fix is a *CLAUDE.md*: a plain text file in your project folder that Claude Code reads automatically at the start of every session.

**Write 3 to 5 rules in it**, each one line, in plain English. Good ones sound like: 'Ask before changing any file I didn't mention.' 'After each change, tell me how to test it in the browser.' 'One feature per request, no extras.'

Grow it slowly. Each time you correct Claude on the same thing twice, that correction becomes a line.
cards.simpler: Every new Claude Code session starts with an empty memory. Yesterday's 'please don't touch the save file' is forgotten. The fix is a file called CLAUDE.md. It's a plain text file in your project folder that Claude Code reads at the start of every session. **Write 3 to 5 rules in it**, one line each. For example: 'Ask before changing any file I didn't mention.' Each time you correct Claude on the same thing twice, that correction becomes a line.

cards.body: Sam finishes Tuesday's session with everything working and closes the terminal. On Wednesday, Claude rewrites the save file again, uninvited, and Sam types the same frustrated correction as yesterday. **Saying the same correction twice is the signal.** The moment you notice you're repeating yourself, stop and put that sentence in CLAUDE.md. Then it's the last time.
cards.simpler: Sam ends Tuesday's session with everything working and closes the terminal. On Wednesday, Claude rewrites the save file again without being asked. Sam types the same annoyed correction as the day before. **Typing the same correction twice is the signal.** The moment you catch yourself repeating a sentence to Claude, stop and put that sentence in CLAUDE.md. Then it's the last time you have to say it.

cards.prompt: You're closing a session. Which of these belongs in your CLAUDE.md file?

options.text: Today I fixed the login bug and added dark mode.
Always ask before changing a file I didn't mention.
The full red error message from this morning.

whyNot.a: That's a diary of what happened, which Git already keeps. The notes file holds rules for how to work, not history.
whyNot.c: That's a one-time problem from chapter 4. It's fixed now; a rule outlives any single error.

cards.reteach: CLAUDE.md is the note for tomorrow's crew, so it holds standing orders: how you want the builder to behave every day. Not what got done, not what broke once.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Claude saying *done* is a claim, not a check. **Click through the app yourself**, ask for the list of changed files and question any surprise, then write the rules you keep repeating into CLAUDE.md so tomorrow's session already knows them.
cards.simpler: When Claude says done, that is a claim, not proof. Those are the three checks. **Click through the app yourself.** Then ask for the list of files that changed and question anything you didn't expect. Finally, write the rules you keep repeating into CLAUDE.md, so tomorrow's session already knows them before you start.

cards.body: Open your project folder, create a file called CLAUDE.md, and type 3 rules you'd want followed tomorrow. Start the first one with 'Ask before...'. Then start Claude Code and ask: *what rules are you following?*
cards.simpler: Open your project folder and make a new file called CLAUDE.md. Type three rules you'd want followed tomorrow, one short line each. **Start the first one with 'Ask before...'** Then start Claude Code and ask it one question: what rules are you following?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now finish a session by testing the app yourself, reading Claude's list of changes, and writing 3 to 5 rules into CLAUDE.md for next time.
